title: AI this week: Friday 6 November 2026
label: Friday 6 November 2026 (sample)
intro: Sample edition. Underlined words lead to short, plain-language explanations. A disclosure: this digest is written by Claude, an AI made by Anthropic, which features in the lead story. Read that story with that in mind.

question.q: How does a chatbot decide which word to write next?
question.teaser: It writes one word at a time, and each time it is making a very well-informed guess.
question.answer: A chatbot turns every word into a long list of numbers, so that words with similar meanings sit close together, like neighbouring towns on a map. Those numbers then pass through many layers, and each layer adds context: whether “bank” means a river bank or a place for money, or who “he” refers to. At the end the model scores every possible next word and picks a likely one. It learned all this simply by practising, on an enormous amount of text, at predicting the next word. The article below explains it with almost no maths. Its authors stress that nobody yet fully understands how these models work inside.
question.source: Timothy B. Lee and Sean Trott, “Large language models, explained with a minimum of math and jargon” (Understanding AI, 2023)

stories.title: Lead story: an outside group says AI is now speeding up its own development
body: METR, an independent nonprofit that evaluates AI, spent about eleven weeks studying internal data at Anthropic and published its report on 5 November. Its best estimate is that Anthropic’s models are now improving about twice as fast as in 2024 and 2025, with a plausible range of roughly 1.3 to 3 times. It judges that most of the speedup, roughly 80%, comes from AI helping with the research itself.
stories.known: The catch: Anthropic removed most of the evidence METR found most informative, so readers have to trust METR’s judgment rather than check it. METR also relied on benchmark test scores, which are an imperfect measure. And it did not show that AI is building itself: people still make the decisions.

stories.email: An independent group, METR, spent about eleven weeks studying internal data at Anthropic and estimates its AI models are now improving about twice as fast as in 2024 and 2025 (plausible range: 1.3 to 3 times), mostly because AI is helping with the research itself. The catch is that Anthropic removed most of the evidence METR found most informative, so readers have to trust METR’s judgment. Anthropic makes Claude, which wrote this email.

stories.title: AI helped find weak spots in an older kind of encryption
body: Google DeepMind said on Thursday that AI models, working alongside human code-breaking experts, found two weaknesses in an older form of RSA, a system that has long protected online transactions. One makes forging digital signatures about 1,600 times more efficient. The other makes cracking many keys at once about 30 times cheaper per extra key.
stories.known: What is and isn’t established: DeepMind says the modern, stronger version is not affected, and no real-world system has been named as vulnerable. This is a research announcement, not a report of a break-in.
stories.email: Google DeepMind says AI models, working with human code-breaking experts, found two weaknesses in an older form of RSA, a system that has long protected online transactions. DeepMind says the modern, stronger version is not affected, and no real-world system has been named as vulnerable. It is a research announcement, not a report of a break-in.

stories.title: How scientific research gets checked is under strain
body: ICLR is one of the field’s major AI research conferences. Every paper submitted is read by volunteer expert reviewers, and the conference is struggling to keep up. In September it capped submissions at 20 papers per author, and at one paper for people who have never published at a major conference, citing a flood of manuscripts that AI tools make easy to produce. Its rules for the 2027 round let reviewers use AI to help write reviews only if they disclose it, and reviews with AI-made errors can lead to penalties, including having the reviewer’s own papers rejected.
stories.known: What is and isn’t established: X is showing a headline today saying this year’s reviews have raised fresh concerns about AI in peer review. I could not confirm what happened today, so the description above is the conference’s own published policy, not a report of this week’s events.
stories.email: A major AI research conference, ICLR, has capped how many papers one person can submit and set rules for reviewers who use AI, because AI tools are flooding the system with paper-like manuscripts. Reviews with AI-made errors can lead to penalties. X shows a headline about fresh concerns this week, but I could not confirm what happened, so this describes the published policy.

stories.title: Listening for patterns in dolphin sounds
body: Scientists are using AI to search decades of dolphin recordings for sounds that repeat in similar situations. No genuine two-way conversation with dolphins has been shown. The achievement is the pattern-finding, which no person could do by hand.

stories.title: Asking a satellite archive questions in plain English
body: The company Planet launched a tool that lets people search about ten years of Earth imagery by describing what they want to see, to track changes over time.

stories.title: OpenAI raises $11 billion, less than it hoped
body: Reuters reported on 6 November, citing sources, that OpenAI has closed $11 billion in new funding at a valuation of $1.25 trillion. This is the first part of a larger round. It is well short of the up-to-$30 billion OpenAI had aimed for, and the valuation is below the $1.5 trillion it had initially sought. SoftBank and MGX took part, according to two investors. Reuters links this to a cooling in investor enthusiasm for AI companies.
stories.known: What is and isn’t established: the figures come from anonymous sources, and the report does not say OpenAI itself confirmed them.
stories.email: Reuters reports, citing sources, that OpenAI has closed $11 billion in new funding at a $1.25 trillion valuation. That is well short of the up-to-$30 billion it aimed for, and Reuters links it to cooling investor enthusiasm for AI companies. The figures come from anonymous sources, and OpenAI is not reported to have confirmed them.

stories.title: Claude agents that “dream”
body: Anthropic’s “dreaming” feature lets AI agents (programs that carry out tasks on their own) review their own past work between jobs. A scheduled process looks across many earlier sessions for patterns, such as repeated mistakes, and writes plain-text notes that later sessions can read. Anthropic says it does not change the underlying model, so people can inspect the notes.
stories.known: What is and isn’t established: Anthropic announced this in May and describes it as a research preview. A big improvement figure quoted at launch came from a customer, not an independent test. X is showing a headline about it today, and I could not tell what is new. Anthropic makes Claude, which wrote this digest.

stories.title: Governments tighten rules on data centers
body: Places from New York to Amsterdam have tightened rules on building data centers, the huge buildings that AI runs in, amid growing local resistance over their power use.
stories.learn: Why data centers are in the news
stories.email: Governments from New York to Amsterdam have tightened rules on building data centers, the huge buildings AI runs in, amid growing local resistance over their power use. It is a quieter form of AI regulation: rules about the buildings and electricity, not the software.

stories.title: A new US Justice Department unit for advanced AI
body: The Justice Department has launched a task force to investigate unlawful uses of advanced AI, with a focus on foreign governments, criminal groups and AI-related fraud.

stories.title: OpenAI announces “GPT-6 Cyber”
body: A model built for security work, such as finding flaws in software and checking fixes. OpenAI rates its capability as “Critical” and, at first, is giving access only to selected organizations. It is the two-sided theme again: tools that find holes can also help close them.

footer_trust: How much to trust this edition: the lead story comes from METR’s own report, the conference item from ICLR’s published policies, and the OpenAI item from a Reuters report. The “dreaming” item comes from a trade-press article about Anthropic’s announcement. The DeepMind, dolphin, satellite, data center, Justice Department and security items come from news summaries (a daily AI newsletter citing outlets including Reuters and WIRED, plus a developer digest), not from the original articles, so treat those details as reported, not independently confirmed.
email_footer: The lead story draws on METR’s own report and the others on a mix of primary and second-hand sources; each page on the website says which. Details are as reported, not independently confirmed.
